name: Forge
text: We should start by building packages for the most commonly used Claude skills, as this will give us the widest reach and allow us to test our process. By focusing on popular skills, we can maximize the value of our work and create a strong foundation for future development. This approach means we'll have to accept the trade-off of potentially leaving some niche skills unaddressed initially, but it's a worthwhile sacrifice for the sake of efficiency and impact. By prioritizing these key skills, we can create a robust set of packages that will benefit the largest number of users.

name: Vet
text: The real risk is chasing popularity over actual need—we might waste time on skills that sound useful but aren’t used in practice. Instead, start with the skills already failing in the wild, where users are stuck and our fixes would matter most. That settles it: measure demand by error logs, not downloads.

name: Forge
text:
Build the package for the "Web Search" skill first. It’s the most frequent failure point in user logs—people get stuck when Claude can’t fetch live data, and fixing this cuts the biggest pain. The trade-off is ignoring less critical skills, but that’s acceptable because fixing the top blocker delivers the most immediate value.

name: Vet
text: The real risk is locking ourselves into a single skill’s failure mode while ignoring systemic gaps—Web Search may dominate logs, but if the fix breaks other integrations, we’ve traded one bottleneck for another. Instead, audit the top *three* failure clusters first; if Web Search tops the list, we’ll still fix it—but only after proving it’s the worst offender, not the loudest. Settle it by pulling the last 30 days of error data, ranking by frequency *and* severity, and letting the numbers—not urgency—decide.

name: Nova
text: DECISION: Audit the top three failure clusters from user logs, then build the Web Search skill package only if it ranks #1—Forge owns the audit and Vet signs off on the ranking before any build starts.
